title: Best Profit from K Trades
statement:
prices[i] is the price of one share on day i. A trade means buying one share on some day and selling it on a later day. You may hold at most one share at a time, so you must sell before you buy again. Selling and buying again on the same day is allowed.

You may make at most k trades. Return the largest total profit you can make. Making no trades at all gives 0.

examples.why: Buy at 3, sell at 8 (+5), buy at 2, sell at 9 (+7). The third rise, 1 to 4, would need a third trade.
With one trade, buy at 2 and hold through the dip to sell at 9. Adding up both rises (4 + 5 = 9) would need two trades.
Prices only fall, so the best plan is not to trade.

hints: Track the best result so far in a few states: how many trades you have started, and whether you are holding a share right now.
For each trade number t, keep two numbers: the best cash after buying for the t-th time (holding), and the best cash after selling for the t-th time (not holding).

On each day, for t from 1 to k: hold[t] = max(hold[t], free[t − 1] − price) and free[t] = max(free[t], hold[t] + price). The answer is free[k]. If k ≥ n / 2, the limit never binds: just add every rise.

explain.intuition:
At any moment your situation is described by two things: how many trades you have started, and whether you are holding a share. For each trade count t, keep the best cash you can have while holding (hold[t]) and while not holding after completing t trades (free[t]). A new day can only change these in two ways: buy, which moves you from free[t − 1] to hold[t] by paying the price, or sell, which moves you from hold[t] to free[t] by receiving it.

That gives O(k) work per day and O(n · k) in total, with O(k) memory. One more observation: a plan never needs more than n / 2 trades, because each trade takes at least two days. So when k ≥ n / 2, the cap is irrelevant and the answer is simply the sum of every day-to-day rise.
steps: If 2k ≥ n, return the sum of max(0, prices[i] − prices[i − 1]) over all days.
For each price p, for t = 1..k: hold[t] = max(hold[t], free[t − 1] − p), then free[t] = max(free[t], hold[t] + p).
pitfalls: Adding every rise when k is small. The second example shows that one long trade can beat the best single rise, and two rises need two trades.
Taking the k biggest separate rises. A long trade that spans a dip can be worth more than two separate rises when trades are scarce.
Running the O(n · k) table with a huge k in variants where k can be 10⁹. The k ≥ n / 2 shortcut is what keeps it fast.

solutions.title: Table over trades and days, trying every buy day
solutions.idea: best[t][i] is the best profit with at most t trades using days 0..i. Either day i is not a sell day, or the last trade buys on some day j and sells on day i.

solutions.title: Hold / free states per trade count
solutions.idea: For each trade count keep the best cash while holding and while free. Each day, try buying and selling for every count.

followups: Every sale now costs a fixed fee. Which line of the state update changes?
k can be up to 10⁹ and n up to 10⁶. Can you solve it in about O(n log n)? (Hint: merge or split the rises greedily with a heap, or binary search a penalty per trade.)
